How to read this report

Each finding is a graded fact about what an app's files hold. The grade says what kind of evidence there is, and a finding takes the highest grade its evidence reaches. No finding says what an app or a company intends.

GradeIn a wordWhat it shows
declaresdeclaresThe app's own files name this endpoint, for example as the address of its update feed or as a domain in its privacy manifest. A declaration is not an observed connection.
containsshipsThe app ships this code. That shows the code is present, not that it runs or sends anything.
contactscontactedThe operating system or a capture recorded a connection.
confirmedconfirmedThe receiver's own records list the app as a sender, or a payload was inspected.
Confidence
How unlikely it is that a marker matched by coincidence. High for a name read from a structured table, medium for text in the app's own code or in a binary's data, low for text inside a bundled library. It is not a score.
Kinds of evidence
How many independent kinds of marker agree, such as a class name and an entry in the app's manifest.
First party, third party
First party: the company is the app's own publisher. Third party: it is someone else.
Component
A library with no network side of its own, such as an updater. It names no company.
Unmapped host
A host the app declares that the rule pack lists under no company. It is shown as itself and nobody is named as its owner.

What was scanned, and what was not

Nothing found is not the same as not looked at. This section says where the scan looked, lists every app it read, and lists everything it set aside or could not interpret.

What this report cannot tell you

This report rests on files that are on the device. It shows what an app ships and what it declares. Three things are out of reach of this scan and of every scan of a device:

  • What is sent. Apps encrypt their traffic, so the content of a request cannot be read from the device. No finding here says which data was sent, or that any was.
  • What companies pass on between their own servers. Sharing from one server to another never touches the device and leaves nothing on it to find.
  • What is sent through the app's own domain. An app can send data to its publisher's servers, which forward it to another company. On the device this looks like the app talking to its publisher.

Four more limits apply to what is reported:

  • Presence is not use. contains means the code is in the app. The code may never run, and the service behind it may be retired. Only a recorded connection, at grade contacts, shows a live flow, and a scan of app files records none.
  • Only what has a rule is recognised. The scanner knows the SDKs its rule pack describes and no others. An app with no finding is not shown to be free of third-party code.
  • Some code hides its markers. Heavily obfuscated code, an encrypted binary, short text inside Swift code and JavaScript compiled to bytecode can each keep an SDK from being recognised. What the scan set aside is listed under coverage.
  • Names are as the files give them. An app's name, its id and the Team ID in its signature are read from the app and are not verified.
